text: Once a workload has a genuine reason to involve a second cloud, the next question is what shape that multi-cloud actually takes, because 'we're going multi-cloud' can mean two very different commitments that get talked about as if they were the same thing. Telling them apart before you build anything is the single most important decision in this lesson.

Best-of-breed multi-cloud means picking the best available service for each individual workload and running that workload on whichever provider offers it, while every other workload stays wherever it already fits best. A company might keep its ERP and identity estate on Azure while routing one specific machine-learning workload to a provider with a better-suited model catalog. The defining trait: each workload still runs on exactly one cloud. Nothing is duplicated. The integration cost is real, but it's bounded to a network path, a shared identity layer, and whatever data the two systems need to exchange.

Redundancy-driven multi-cloud is a different thing entirely: running the same workload, in parallel or hot standby, on two different providers, so a provider-wide outage can't take it down. That's active-active when both copies serve real traffic, or active-passive when one sits ready to take over. It's genuinely more resilient against one specific failure mode a single-cloud design can't cover. It's also genuinely more expensive, because now every change has to be designed, built, and validated twice, kept behaviorally equal across two completely separate implementations.

That cost difference is why the two get conflated so often and why conflating them is a mistake. Best-of-breed multi-cloud scales its cost with the number of workloads involved, since each one is still a single implementation. Redundancy-driven multi-cloud roughly doubles the engineering, testing, and on-call cost of whatever single workload it's applied to, which is why it belongs on the small number of workloads where an extended outage is genuinely existential, not as a default resilience pattern.

So before approving any multi-cloud proposal, make it answer directly: is a workload simply moving to the provider that handles it better, or is the same workload being built twice to survive an outage? Next, Lesson 7 puts real numbers behind that second option — the duplicated tooling, duplicated skills, and duplicated security and monitoring posture it actually costs an organization to run.
